articles.title: In 2012, Jeff Gordon’s foundation helped open a cancer centre in Rwanda; by 2025, it had seen more than 18,000 patients and helped build care where treatment had once been almost out of reach
articles.summary: A cancer diagnosis can change a life in an instant, but in Rwanda, access to treatment was once so limited that many patients had little chance of
articles.body: A cancer diagnosis can change a life in an instant, but in Rwanda, access to treatment was once so limited that many patients had little chance of survival. A centre established in 2012 helped change that reality, bringing cancer treatment, medical training and research to a country where specialist care was scarce. Race car driver Jeff Gordon’s foundation contributed to the opening of the Butaro Cancer Center of Excellence, an initiative that has since treated more than 18,000 patients. According to Harvard Medicine Magazine, which documented the centre’s development in May 2025, the facility has also helped strengthen cancer screening programmes and train healthcare professionals, demonstrating how locally delivered care can expand access to treatment in resource-limited settings.Why Rwanda needed a dedicated cancer centreWhen Rwanda began developing its cancer treatment infrastructure in 2011, the country faced a serious shortage of specialist services. According to the Harvard Medicine report, there were no medical oncologists or radiotherapy facilities at the time, and pathology services were limited. Doctors struggled to provide sustained treatment to patients, including children with cancer. Cyprien Shyirambere, a paediatrician who later became the oncology director for Partners In Health in Rwanda, recalled seeing young patients who could receive enough chemotherapy to enter remission temporarily but could not access the continued care they needed.Recognising this gap, the Rwandan government invited Dana-Farber Brigham Cancer Center and Partners In Health (PIH) to collaborate on establishing a comprehensive cancer centre in Butaro, in the Northern Province. The initiative aimed to create the first centre of its kind in East Africa. The project built on PIH’s existing work in Rwanda, where the organisation had been supporting healthcare services since 2005. Jeff Gordon’s foundation was among the contributors to the cancer centre’s opening, alongside the wider partnership involving medical institutions, local healthcare professionals and the Rwandan government.How the Butaro centre changed cancer careThe Butaro Cancer Center of Excellence opened in 2012. More than 1,000 patients received treatment during its first year, and the centre had seen over 18,000 patients by the time Harvard Medicine reported on its progress in 2025. The transformation involved more than constructing a medical facility. The team worked to establish the systems needed to diagnose and treat cancer, including clinical protocols, surgical capabilities and training for local staff.Initially, the centre lacked pathologists who could process biopsy samples locally. Tissue samples had to be sent to Boston for processing and examination. Over time, healthcare workers received specialist training, allowing the centre to develop its own pathology capacity. By 2025, two histopathologists were working on site, and around 90% of samples were being read in Butaro. The centre also developed regular discussions among specialists to review complex cases and support continuing medical education. These efforts helped build local expertise rather than relying entirely on visiting doctors.Research helped improve early diagnosisCancer treatment depends not only on access to medicines but also on identifying the disease early enough for treatment to be effective. Research conducted by Lydia Pace and her colleagues identified significant delays in diagnosing breast cancer in Rwanda. One early study found that women experienced delays of around 15 months between noticing symptoms and receiving a diagnosis.Limited awareness, concerns about treatment costs and the practical difficulties of attending appointments contributed to the problem. Specialist diagnostic resources, including mammography machines and radiologists, were also scarce. To address these barriers, clinicians developed a programme that trained general practitioners, nurses and midwives to use ultrasound for breast cancer assessment. The approach helped expand access to diagnostic services without requiring specialist radiologists at every location.According to the Harvard report, the Rwandan government subsequently expanded the early-diagnosis programme to cover 60% of the country's districts. The broader importance of the project is also reflected in a 2020 review published in the journal Cancer Control, titled State of Cancer Control in Rwanda: Past, Present, and Future Opportunities. The paper describes Rwanda’s progress in cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment, while highlighting the continuing need to strengthen national cancer services.Progress continues, but challenges remainThe centre’s achievements have not eliminated the difficulties associated with cancer treatment in Rwanda. High drug costs, delays in diagnosis and treatment, and shortages of specialist surgeons continue to affect outcomes. The Harvard report noted that the survival rate for Hodgkin’s lymphoma in Rwanda had risen to approximately 50%, compared with around 90% in the United States, illustrating both the progress made and the gap that remains.Funding is another concern. Research, training and healthcare initiatives have received support from international partners and government programmes, making long-term sustainability an important consideration. Nevertheless, the Butaro Cancer Center of Excellence has demonstrated how partnerships can help build healthcare capacity where specialist services were previously limited. Its contribution extends beyond the patients treated within its walls to the clinicians trained, diagnostic programmes developed and lessons that can inform cancer care elsewhere.Jeff Gordon’s foundation helped support the centre’s opening, but its continuing work reflects a broader collective effort. More than a decade after it opened, Butaro stands as an example of how sustained investment in local expertise, research and accessible treatment can change the possibilities available to people facing cancer.You use AI every day. articles.title: A British woman sought £135,000 for caring for her mother for 900 days; the High Court awarded her £127,500 plus interest after finding an informal care agreement existed
articles.summary: A British woman has been awarded £127,500 plus interest from her late mother’s estate after the High Court upheld her claim for years of unpaid care.
articles.body: A British woman has been awarded £127,500 plus interest from her late mother’s estate after the High Court upheld her claim for years of unpaid care. Bernadette Rogers had initially sought £135,000, arguing that her mother, Ursula Wills, known as Sheila, had agreed to pay her a reasonable sum for looking after her in her later years. According to the High Court judgment, handed down on 25 August 2026, the court found that a binding informal contract existed between mother and daughter. The ruling followed a dispute with Rogers’s brother, the executor of their mother’s estate, over the amount payable for the care provided.How did a daughter claim £135,000 for caring for her motherRogers’s mother, Ursula Wills, was known within the family as Sheila. She was born in Birkenhead on 26 August 1927 and had lived with her husband, John Wills, in Southrepps, near Cromer on the East Anglian coast, for many years. After her husband died in 2012, Sheila eventually became unable to continue living independently because of her frailty, forgetfulness and episodes of confusion. In September 2017, she moved into the Bristol home of Rogers and her husband, Dr Rogers, a retired general practitioner.The earlier liability judgment found that the agreement was reached in October 2017. According to the findings reproduced in the August 2026 judgment, Sheila wanted to pay for the care she received rather than depend on charity. HHJ Matthews recorded that Sheila had insisted that her return to Bristol would be on terms that she “wanted to pay her way” and that Rogers would be “paid properly” for looking after her. The judgment stated that there had been no discussion about a specific amount, with the sum to be determined later. The court concluded that the absence of an agreed figure did not prevent the arrangement from constituting a contract for services at a reasonable price.How did Rogers care for her mother until her deathRogers was found to have been the principal carer for her mother during the relevant period. Sheila lived in the family’s Bristol home from September 2017 until her death on 19 April 2020. The judgment described her as suffering from several health conditions, including vascular dementia, diabetes, angina, chronic kidney disease, glaucoma and recurring rectal prolapse. She also experienced impaired mobility, incontinence and periods of confusion. The court accepted Rogers’s evidence that her mother required continuous supervision and that either Rogers or her husband generally had to remain at home with her.The care included preparing meals, cleaning, doing laundry, helping with washing and toileting, managing medication and arranging medical appointments. Rogers also provided companionship, reassurance and activities, while helping to manage her mother’s medical conditions. The court found that the arrangement affected Rogers’s household routine and prevented her from continuing to care for her grandchildren for payment two days a week. The family also incurred additional expenses associated with accommodation, heating, utilities, food, transport and other household needs. During the final weeks of Sheila’s life, after she suffered a fall on 2 April 2020 and sustained a head injury, fractured ribs and a fractured hip, Rogers and her husband worked in shifts to care for her. Sheila died at their home on 19 April 2020.Why did the High Court award £127,500 instead of £135,000Rogers sought payment at a rate of £150 a day for 900 days, amounting to £135,000. However, the court identified a distinction between the total period during which care had been provided and the period covered by the contract. Although the evidence established 900 days of care, the agreement was found to have been formed on or around 2 November 2017. The contractual period was therefore 850 days. The court assessed the claim on that basis rather than awarding the full amount initially sought.In determining reasonable payment, the court considered evidence about the cost of obtaining comparable care from commercial providers, including live-in care services and nursing homes. It also examined the defendant’s proposed valuation, which was based on local government care-worker pay rates and a lower estimate of the number of hours of care required each day. District Judge Wales concluded that the evidence supported a live-in care comparison, taking account of supervision, personal assistance, medical and dementia care, overnight support, accommodation and travel. The judgment stated: “I am satisfied that the sum claimed by the Claimant represents a reasonable contractual charge for the services she in fact provided.” The court ultimately awarded Rogers £127,500, together with interest, and ruled that her claim succeeded.You use AI every day. articles.title: NMC denotifies medical education rules; annual disclosures risk lacking verification
articles.summary: National Medical Commission has denotified the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023.
articles.body: National Medical Commission has denotified the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023. With the denotification, all specific penalties against medical institutions that fail to comply with any of the statutory provisions and regulations or minimum standards are no longer applicable.Any action taken while the regulations were in force would not be affected. However, NMC has not taken any action against many colleges flouting regulations as in the case of non-payment of stipend to MBBS interns and doctors doing PG. Colleges will now have little to fear if they do not pay stipend as the penalty for is not specified in the NMC Act.Without evaluation, med colleges’ disclosure would just be unverified claimsThe Act only states that the Medical Assessment and Rating Board shall take such measures, including issuing warning, imposition of monetary penalty, reducing intake or stoppage of admissions or recommendation for withdrawal of recognition against a medical institution for failure to maintain the minimum essential standards specified.“Notwithstanding such denotification, the requirement of furnishing the annual disclosure report shall continue to operate” in accordance with relevant sections of NMC Act 2019, read the denotification announcement gazetted on Oct 14. NMC Act stipulates that the UnderGraduate Medical Education Board and the Post-Graduate Medical Education Board shall specify norms for compulsory annual disclosures by medical institutions.The 2019 Act also states that MARB may conduct evaluation of any institute at any time without prior notice. However, with the denotification, the aspects that need to be included in the evaluation report, such as verification of physical infrastructure, availability of the required number of faculty and review of feedback from students, have also been removed.Without evaluation by MARB, the mandated annual disclosure would just be claims by a medical college unverified by an independent assessment.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Tiger shooters got weapons via ‘dead drop’; couriers delivered guns a day earlier
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The shooters involved in the attack on actor Tiger Shroff received their weapons through a “dead drop” arrangement on Oct 17, just a day before
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The shooters involved in the attack on actor Tiger Shroff received their weapons through a “dead drop” arrangement on Oct 17, just a day before the incident. Couriers Babita and Radha — who have since been arrested — were provided the weapons at New Delhi Railway Station by the main supplier, identified as Kunal.Kunal, who has also been arrested, has emerged as a key character who had been in touch with gangsters Anil Pandit and Randeep Malik for over two months. He had also figured as the source of the weapon used for the murder of a forex-hawala trader in Sonipat last year, sources said.In this case, he was relaying the instructions from Pandit to the two women after dropping them at the station on Oct 15. The women reached Mumbai on Oct 17, got off at Dadar and checked into a hotel. Around 11am, one of the shooters collected the bag with the weapons at an isolated spot near the hotel, an official added.The dead drop method — borrowed from spycraft — has increasingly surfaced in investigations involving terror modules, drug cartels and organised crime groups of late. Agencies have unearthed non-contact logistics where handlers use encrypted messaging to direct operatives to pre-arranged locations to collect weapons, funds and synthetic drugs. Some cases in point include IS-linked terror modules, cross-border drone-dropped payloads along the Punjab and J&K frontiers, interstate gang firearm procurements and synthetic drug delivery networks.Investigators reconstruct digital footprints, chat logs and GPS coordinates alongside CCTV footage analysis to establish the timeline. By using technical surveillance, cell tower dumps and financial intelligence tied to encrypted communications, agencies are able to intercept these isolated drop routines to cut off unverified supplier-courier links, sources said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Drug menace next target, says Union home minister Amit Shah; eyes 2029 deadline
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Stating that peace had been established in the country’s three primary hotspots — Jammu & Kashmir, the Northeast region and areas affected by
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Stating that peace had been established in the country’s three primary hotspots — Jammu & Kashmir, the Northeast region and areas affected by left-wing extremism (LWE) — Union home minister Amit Shah Wednesday said the home ministry is now focused on the drug menace and aims to make the country narcotics-free by Dec 31, 2029. Addressing an event in the national capital to mark Police Commemoration Day, Shah said 2026 had been an extremely significant year for the Indian police, as they successfully freed the country from the decades-old stranglehold of violent Naxalism.Stating that an environment conducive to development has emerged in Kashmir, Northeast and LWE-hit regions, Shah particularly thanked CRPF and its CoBRA battalion as well as Chhattisgarh Police for their role in the decisive fight against LWE.The home ministry will dedicate the remaining part of 2026 and three years after that to freeing the country from the drug menace, Shah said and called upon police forces across the country to wholeheartedly participate in the implementation of the ‘nasha-mukt Bharat’ roadmap. The home minister also flagged off a nationwide motorcycle rally with the theme ‘fight against drugs’. Five riders each from 36 states/Union territories and 9 CAPFs are participating in this rally and will reach Kevadia, Gujarat, from different parts of the country, to join the Ekta Diwas parade on Oct 31.On the occasion of Police Commemoration Day, Shah placed a wreath at National Police Memorial to honour the 36,852 personnel who laid down their lives so far in the line of duty.7,000 from LWE-hit districts to attend Ekta Diwas paradeThe end of armed Naxalism within the March 31, 2026 deadline set by Union home minister Amit Shah as well 150 years of ‘Vande Mataram’ will be celebrated at the Rashtriya Ekta Diwas parade and Bharat Parv at Kevadia, Gujarat, this year to mark Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel’s birth anniversary on Oct 31.Around 7,000 people from 126 districts who were under the scourge of left-wing extremism will participate both as performers and spectators in the event to be attended by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.In addition, around 5,000 local people from these 126 districts across the country have been invited.“Their participation will underline the resilience of communities that have endured conflict and highlight the role of cultural expression in strengthening national integration,” Union home secretary Govind Mohan said.The parade will also feature march-past by contingents of all the CAPFs and state police personnel who fought against LWE violence.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: A few days in the year line up well for Cancer, starting this Thursday. It is Papankusha Ekadashi on Jupiter’s weekday, and Jupiter itself is exalted on your lagna. By evening, your ruler, the Moon, enters Pisces, your ninth house of dharma and fortune, in Purva Bhadrapada, a nakshatra Jupiter also rules. Exalted Jupiter’s gaze reaches that house as well, wrapping the Moon in its blessing. articles.title: Cars to brake on their own: Centre plans AEBS mandate from Oct 2030
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Certain safety features of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) will be made mandatory for cars, particularly taxis, as govt steps up
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Certain safety features of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) will be made mandatory for cars, particularly taxis, as govt steps up efforts to reduce road crashes. From Oct 2030, all new car models would be required to be equipped with the advanced emergency braking system (AEBS), the most important ADAS feature, TOI has learnt.As for pre-2030 still-in production models, AEBS would mandatory from Oct 2032.The draft notification, with timelines for different ADAS safety features for cars, would be out soon, people aware of the development said, adding that focus would be more on taxis. They said the proposed timelines take into account the lead time that industry and users would need.ADAS is a set of more than 100 electronic technologies that increases safety by detecting potential hazards, warning the driver, and in some cases, automatically controlling brakes or steering to prevent a collision. At present, some cars have ADAS.Starting Jan 2027, new truck and bus models will have AEBS — it detects an imminent collision with a vehicle or obstacle and automatically applies brakes, if the driver fails to respond adequately, preventing a crash or reducing its severity. Blind spot information, moving off information and driver drowsiness detection and alert, and lane departure warning systems have been also made mandatory for these commercial vehicles.It’s learnt that features, including automatic command steering functionalities, emergency lane keeping system, drowsiness and attention warning systems, would be made mandatory for taxis.The introduction of these norms could initially focus on ensuring compliance with Automotive Industry Standards for vehicles already equipped with AEBS or more advanced systems that can intervene in steering and lane-keeping, said Automobile and mobility expert Rama Pandey. “These technologies could prove a boon for commercial drivers who spend hours behind the wheel. By shifting more safety-critical & fatigue-inducing driving decisions to automated systems, ADAS could make driving safer and less strenuous,” he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: Sienna Miller’s dreamy thatched cottage, with its thatched roof, flint walls and wildflowers creeping towards the front door, looks straight out of a fantasy film. The 1,922 sq ft home, known as Thatch, is on the market for £1.75 million, according to the listing on Savills. The property was initially offered for £1.95 million. The asking price has since been reduced by £200,000, Country Living reported.Buckinghamshire’s thatched cottageSienna Miller bought the property in 2008, when London had started to wear her down. She has said she was looking for somewhere to slow down. “I was in London and life was very tense, and I was just dreaming about having a place to get away to,” she told Architectural Digest. After coming across the cottage online, she went to see it and “fell completely in love”. The cottage sits in the Buckinghamshire hamlet of Toweridge, in the Chiltern Hills, close to the village of West Wycombe.A 16th-century house with a lot of characterThatch is a traditional 16th-century English cottage nestled in a tranquil rural estate. It is Grade II listed, which means the building’s historic character is protected, and that tends to shape what an owner can change. The listing describes the cottage as a “rare gem, beautifully combining period charm with modern country living”. Built from traditional flint and brick, with Tudor-style timber framing on one side, the cottage “exudes timeless character”.While most people tend to straighten things out when renovating a house, Miller chose to preserve its character. She asked her close friend, director Gaby Dellal, to work on the interiors. They kept everything that made the place unique: the low ceilings, the uneven walls and the centuries-old beams. The renovation resulted in a warm, characterful and personal country home rather than a pristine celebrity show house.Inside ThatchThe 1,922 sq ft thatched cottage sits on 0.57 acres of land. Property agent Hugh Maconochie of Savills described it as “a charming cottage in a private estate location”. The cottage has four bedrooms beneath the thatched roof, with dormer windows overlooking the surrounding landscape. Miller redecorated the interior and added modern amenities. The principal suite features a freestanding bath, an en suite shower room and a private balcony.“Toweridge itself is a quiet hamlet and the picturesque setting offers a peaceful rural lifestyle, while remaining conveniently close to essential amenities and transport links. Dating from the 16th century, the cottage has history in abundance yet the thoughtful interiors and outdoor seating areas are perfectly placed for family gatherings. If you close your eyes and imagine a quintessential thatch cottage, this is surely it,” Maconochie told The Spaces.The kitchen is just as whimsical. “At the heart of the home is a stylish country kitchen, thoughtfully designed with a Lacanche range cooker, herringbone tiled flooring and French doors that open directly onto the garden, inviting the outdoors in,” the listing says. The kitchen flows into the dining room, which features a large open-hearth fireplace with a brick surround. The ceiling beams are painted, and the original wooden floorboards run throughout the cottage, giving it a rustic charm.Near the galleried landing is a cosy snug. An adjoining room, currently used as a twin bedroom, also offers flexibility. French doors open onto the secluded patio terrace, surrounded by mature trees and lawn.“Outside, the gardens are a haven of natural beauty, with a wildflower meadow, lawns and a pond, which each enhance the peaceful countryside setting,” the listing says. Miller transformed the former gravel driveway and parking area into a wildflower meadow, giving the cottage an even more romantic, storybook setting.Hugh Maconochie and Eddie Hamilton of Savills hold the listing. The quintessential thatched cottage was initially offered for £1.95 million before its price was reduced. The guide price now stands at £1.75 million. It is an English cottage straight out of a fantasy film, set in a rural estate yet equipped with modern features and close to essential amenities and transport links.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Super Typhoon Champi becomes one of 2026’s strongest storms as it heads toward Taiwan and eastern China
articles.summary: Super Typhoon Champi is tied as the strongest tropical cyclone of 2026, with peak winds of 185 mph. Though weakening, it could bring up to 18 inches of rain,...
articles.body:
Super Typhoon Champi, which is barreling across the western Pacific Ocean, became one of the strongest storms on Earth in 2026 on Wednesday.

The tropical cyclone tied April's Super Typhoon Sinlaku for the strongest 1-minute sustained winds of 2026, at 185 mph, which is equivalent to a Category 5 hurricane.

Hurricanes and typhoons are both tropical cyclones with sustained winds of at least 74 mph.

"A tropical cyclone is a generic term used by meteorologists to describe a rotating, organized system of clouds and thunderstorms that originates over tropical or subtropical waters and has closed, low-level circulation," according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration .

The main difference between hurricanes and typhoons is geographic: Storms in the Northwest Pacific are called typhoons, while those in the North Atlantic and central and eastern North Pacific are called hurricanes.

The Joint Typhoon Warning Center classifies a storm as a super typhoon when its 1-minute sustained winds reach at least 150 mph. That threshold falls within the Category 4 hurricane range.

Champi is currently east of the Philippines and southeast of Taiwan, moving west-northwest across the Philippine Sea at 15 mph. Maximum sustained winds are at 175 mph, after peaking at 185 mph, according to the latest update from the National Weather Service .

The storm is forecast to make a slight turn toward the northwest and weaken through Thursday.

Champi is expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Taiwan and eastern China through the weekend, according to AccuWeather senior meteorologist Jason Nicholls.

Heavy rain is expected to affect Taiwan from Thursday night (Oct. 22) into Saturday (Oct. 24) and east-central China from Friday night (Oct. 23) through Sunday (Oct. 25). Rainfall is forecast to total up to 18 inches, with the heaviest rain expected in northeastern Taiwan.

The heavy rain could cause flooding, mudslides, structural damage and transportation delays, according to AccuWeather.

Strong winds from Champi, with wind gusts up to 120 mph, are expected to affect Taiwan and eastern China from Thursday night into Sunday. The winds could cause structural damage, prolonged power outages and transportation delays.

articles.title: Cincinnati’s 1948 Terrace Plaza Hotel has sat vacant since 2008; after two years of asbestos and mold removal, a tax valuation fight is now threatening another attempt to redevelop the landmark
articles.summary: Cincinnati’s historic Terrace Plaza Hotel has been vacant since 2008, but a $160 million plan to bring the 1948 landmark back to life is now facing a new
articles.body: Cincinnati’s historic Terrace Plaza Hotel has been vacant since 2008, but a $160 million plan to bring the 1948 landmark back to life is now facing a new obstacle. After two years of asbestos and mould removal, the redevelopment is being held up by a dispute over the building’s property tax valuation. The case involves the hotel’s owner, a tax valuation appeal and the city’s school district, and has been reported by Blue Water Healthy Living and documented in federal court records.A landmark with a remarkable pastThe Terrace Plaza Hotel was completed in 1948 and designed by Skidmore, Owings and Merrill (SOM), making it the firm’s first hotel project. At 18 storeys and about 600,000 square feet, it was one of the first modern hotels in the United States and a striking addition to downtown Cincinnati. The building was innovative from the start. Its lobby was located on the eighth floor and reached by express elevators from street level, while the first seven floors originally housed department stores. The top floor contained a small gourmet restaurant with panoramic views of the city. The hotel also incorporated major works of modern art. Joan Miró designed a mural for the restaurant, Alexander Calder’s mobile hung in the lobby and Saul Steinberg created a mural for the main restaurant. These artistic features helped make the Terrace Plaza a nationally significant example of mid-century design, as per SOM.From decline to redevelopment hopesThe hotel closed in 2008 and has remained empty ever since, as per reports. Over time, the vacant building developed serious environmental and maintenance problems, including asbestos and mould, which made any future use more difficult and expensive.A redevelopment plan valued at about $160 million aimed to restore the landmark and give it a new economic purpose, reports suggest. Before that vision could move forward, the project team spent roughly two years removing asbestos and mould from the building, an essential step in making the structure safe for renovation. But the cleanup has not resolved the project’s financial uncertainty. A dispute over the hotel’s tax valuation has created another delay, raising concerns that the redevelopment could stall before construction begins.Why the tax valuation mattersAt the centre of the dispute is the assessed value of the Terrace Plaza Hotel. Property taxes are based on valuation, and for a large vacant historic building, even a modest difference in assessed value can translate into a substantial annual tax bill.The owner challenged the valuation, arguing that the building’s condition and vacancy should be reflected in its taxable value. The city’s school district, which depends on property-tax revenue, opposed the reduction, setting up a legal conflict that has now affected the redevelopment timeline.The case has moved through the courts, including the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, which issued a ruling in the matter in March 2023. The litigation illustrates how tax disputes can become a major barrier for complex historic redevelopment projects, particularly when public revenue and private investment are both at stake.What is at stakeThe Terrace Plaza is more than an empty office tower or former hotel. It is a piece of Cincinnati’s architectural and cultural history, with direct connections to some of the most influential artists and designers of the 20th century.If the $160 million redevelopment proceeds, it could remove a long-vacant building from the city’s list of problem properties and return a major downtown structure to active use. The project could also preserve the landmark’s historic character while adapting it for modern needs.If the tax dispute is not resolved, however, the building could remain vacant for longer, leaving the city with the ongoing costs and risks associated with an unused historic structure. The case has become a test of whether Cincinnati can turn a celebrated but troubled landmark into a viable redevelopment project.A familiar challenge for old buildingsThe Terrace Plaza’s situation reflects a common dilemma in historic preservation. Older buildings often need expensive environmental remediation, structural upgrades and modern systems before they can be reused. At the same time, their tax treatment, ownership complications and financing needs can delay even well-supported plans.For Cincinnati, the next stage will depend on how the valuation dispute is resolved and whether the project team can secure the financial certainty needed to move ahead. The building’s artistic legacy and architectural importance give the redevelopment a strong case for preservation, but the legal and financial hurdles remain real.After nearly two decades of vacancy, the Terrace Plaza Hotel stands at a crossroads. Its future now depends not only on construction plans and restoration work, but also on whether city officials, the school district and the owner can find a resolution that allows the landmark’s next chapter to begin.You use AI every day. articles.title: Miami woman sought at least $35 million from Northern Trust over alleged mishandling of her $20 million family trust
articles.summary: Elizabeth Madden, who was 81 when she filed her lawsuit in January 2026, alleges that Northern Trust failed to protect her family’s roughly $20 million
articles.body: Elizabeth Madden, who was 81 when she filed her lawsuit in January 2026, alleges that Northern Trust failed to protect her family’s roughly $20 million legacy trust from unauthorised transactions by a former employee. Her complaint says Christopher Walters, a former vice president and senior fiduciary relationship adviser at the bank, used money from the account to pay credit-card debts and expenses associated with a fitness gym he operated. Madden is seeking at least $35 million in damages from Northern Trust, accusing the bank of failing to prevent the alleged misconduct. Walters is not a defendant in her lawsuit against the bank, but he faces separate civil proceedings brought by Northern Trust and federal criminal charges. He pleaded not guilty in July 2026 to eight counts of bank fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft. Northern Trust has said it was also a victim of Walters’ alleged conduct and disputes Madden’s claims about its responsibility.Lawsuit alleges unauthorised transfers from a family trustMadden’s family had a longstanding relationship with Northern Trust. Her grandfather founded Security Trust Company, a Miami bank acquired by Northern Trust in 1971. The family’s connection to the institution helps explain why Madden continued to entrust her assets to it for decades, according to published reporting. Madden filed her lawsuit against The Northern Trust Company on January 28, 2026, in the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida. The complaint identifies Walters as a former vice president and senior fiduciary relationship adviser who worked at Northern Trust from 2000 to 2024. According to the complaint, Walters transferred money from Madden’s trust without authorisation and directed payments towards credit-card accounts under his control. The alleged transactions continued over more than a decade. The lawsuit accuses Northern Trust of failing to maintain adequate safeguards over trust payments and alleges that the bank collected more than $1 million in fees while the misconduct continued.Madden’s lawyers at Carlton Fields describe the case as an elder financial abuse claim involving alleged unauthorised transfers from a legacy trust. The firm’s announcement of the lawsuit identifies the damages sought as at least $35 million. Northern Trust disputes Madden’s account of its role. The bank has maintained that it was a victim of Walters’ alleged fraud, arguing that an employer cannot be expected to be immune to dishonest employees. Madden’s lawyer, Lee Stapleton, told the Miami Herald that Northern Trust had provided at least three different estimates of the amount allegedly taken. The competing positions remain part of the civil dispute, rather than established findings that Northern Trust itself stole money from Madden.Alleged misconduct surfaced after a change of banksMadden transferred her account to Grove Bank & Trust in Miami in early 2025. According to reporting by the Miami Herald, the alleged misconduct came to light in connection with the transition. The timing of the discovery has also been discussed by Madden’s lawyer, so it should not be treated as an independently established finding about when Northern Trust first learned of the alleged transactions. Walters was terminated in autumn 2024. Northern Trust subsequently filed its own civil lawsuit against him in federal court in August 2025. That case, The Northern Trust Company v. Walters, is separate from Madden’s lawsuit against the bank.In its case against Walters, Northern Trust referred to the affected client as a “Client-Victim” rather than naming Madden. The bank alleged that Walters repeatedly lied to a client while acting outside his authority and abusing his position. The case proceeded after Walters failed to respond. The court docket records a clerk’s entry of default on December 29, 2025, followed by a final default judgment in Northern Trust’s favour. Published reporting states that a federal judge entered the judgment in February 2026, awarding the bank $75,001. A default judgment can be entered when a defendant fails to respond to a lawsuit. The judgment in Northern Trust’s case against Walters does not resolve Madden’s separate claims against the bank or establish that Northern Trust is liable for her alleged losses.Court rejects Northern Trust’s motion to dismissNorthern Trust filed a motion seeking dismissal of Madden’s complaint in February 2026, arguing that it should not be held liable for the alleged scheme. The motion was described in legal reporting as a request to dismiss certain claims, rather than an attempt to end the entire case. On July 13, 2026, the court heard oral arguments on the motion. In an order entered on July 14, Judge Jacqueline Becerra denied Northern Trust’s motion to dismiss. The order also addressed discovery disputes, granting Madden’s request to compel the deposition of a Northern Trust employee and setting deadlines for further discovery. The ruling allowed Madden’s claims to continue, but it did not establish that her allegations were true.The court had earlier granted part of Madden’s request to expedite the trial schedule because of her age. On March 2, the judge directed the parties to confer and submit a joint scheduling report proposing an expedited schedule. That order did not itself set a specific trial date. The parties were subsequently directed to attend mediation by August 6, 2026. The publicly accessible docket information reviewed for this article does not establish the outcome of that mediation, so no settlement or failed mediation is asserted here. The latest docket entries available in the reviewed record can be checked through the federal case docket for Elizabeth Madden v. The Northern Trust Company.Former adviser pleads not guilty to federal chargesWalters’ criminal case is separate from both civil lawsuits. According to the Miami Herald and ThinkAdvisor’s July 9 report, Walters pleaded not guilty in early July 2026 to eight counts of bank fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft. Prosecutors allege that Walters falsified emails and documents submitted to Northern Trust employees to generate fraudulent checks and wire transfers from a client’s account. The indictment does not name Madden or Northern Trust, although media reports have linked the criminal proceedings to the allegations in Madden’s civil lawsuit.The Miami Herald reported that the alleged scheme involved approximately $3 million across about 200 transactions over roughly a decade. Walters is accused of using money from the client’s account to pay credit-card debts and rent for his fitness gym. The figures describe different aspects of the dispute: Madden’s trust was valued at roughly $20 million, the alleged theft is reported at approximately $3 million, and her lawsuit seeks at least $35 million in damages. The damages sought should not be confused with the amount allegedly taken.Walters is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in the criminal case. Madden’s allegations against Northern Trust also remain subject to the civil proceedings. The case raises questions about how financial institutions monitor advisers who manage client assets over many years. Madden’s lawsuit will examine whether Northern Trust met its responsibilities in overseeing the account and responding to the alleged transactions. The separate criminal case will address the charges against Walters, while Northern Trust’s civil action seeks to hold its former employee accountable.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: New norms for DL: Driving tutorial pass mark may rise to 75%, select licence services to be free
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Road transport ministry has proposed raising the pass mark for safe-driving tutorial assessment from 60% to 75% and waiving fees for specified
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Road transport ministry has proposed raising the pass mark for safe-driving tutorial assessment from 60% to 75% and waiving fees for specified driving-licence services availed through online Aadhaar authentication, along with charges for changes to licence particulars such as name and address.The proposed changes to driving licence rules are aimed at tightening assessment requirements and to ensure availing licence-related services without any hassle. The changes proposed in the draft notification to amend sections of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules published late Wednesday night also seek to streamline online driving licence services, specify acceptable identity and residence documents, and introduce time limits for processing applications to change licence particulars.Under the proposal, the safe-driving tutorial would have to last at least 30 minutes. The higher qualifying score of 70% is aimed at making the assessment more stringent. The draft also proposes a defined procedure for online applications to change driving licence particulars, including name and address. Licencing authorities would have to approve or reject applications for changes within 15 days, giving reasons for rejection.An application for an address change that remains undecided for 30 days would be deemed approved.The proposed rules also specify documents that can be submitted as proof of identity, age and residence. These include Aadhaar, passport, voter identity card, recognised educational certificates and birth certificates, among other documents. Electricity and household gas bills not older than three months are among the proposed address-proof documents. LIC policy would no more be accepted as a proof.The draft also provides for a consolidated application form covering services such as licence renewal, issuance of duplicate licences, addition of a vehicle class and changes to personal particulars. Specified applicant details would be retrieved electronically from the SARATHI portal wherever available.In another proposed change, a vehicle class would be deleted from a driving licence within seven days of an application to surrender it. However, applicants permanently surrendering a class would not be eligible to obtain a learner’s or driving licence for that class for one year.The draft notification invites objections and suggestions from stakeholders within 30 days of publication. The proposals will come into force after final notification.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Why are uninsured vehicles not part of crash relief scheme? Supreme Court
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: With Centre formulating a scheme to provide interim financial relief of Rs 2 lakh to families of road crash victims for deaths and Rs 1 lakh
articles.body: NEW DELHI: With Centre formulating a scheme to provide interim financial relief of Rs 2 lakh to families of road crash victims for deaths and Rs 1 lakh for grievous injuries, limited to accidents involving insured vehicles, SC has sought an explanation from govt on why it is not being extended to uninsured vehicles.Taking note that “Compensation to Victims (Interim Relief) Scheme, 2026” has not been notified or publicised, a bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and KV Viswanathan directed the govt to publicise it to ensure awareness. People must be made aware of their right to seek interim compensation, it said.Union road transport ministry officials said the scheme will be notified as provided for under Central Motor Vehicle Act. Govt informed SC that the ministry shared the scheme with states and UTs on Feb 23. SC had directed the ministry in April 2025 to formulate the scheme.On why it covers only insured vehicles, officials said it was framed under provisions of MV Act dealing with insured vehicles. If the offender’s vehicle is uninsured, the matter will go to a Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT).The apex court bench examined clause 6 of the scheme, which specifies that victims or legal heirs of the deceased can apply through a designated online portal, providing details of claims filed or pending before a MACT.Officials said that Section 164 of the Act, which deals with compensation in cases of death or grievous injury, requires the vehicle owner or insurer to pay Rs 5 lakh and Rs 2.5 lakh for death and serious injury, respectively, under the “no-fault liability” provision. A claimant need not establish that death or injury resulted from wrongful act, neglect or default on the vehicle owner’s part.“Hence, interim relief was set at Rs 2 lakh for death and Rs 1 lakh for serious injury for immediate relief. Final compensation would be higher, depending on the order of MACT,” an official said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1940, a Texas family acquired the ranch where generations grew pecan trees and spent holidays; 86 years later, they sold its 650 lakefront acres for more than $10 million so the land can become a state park
articles.summary: A family-owned ranch on Lake Palestine in East Texas is set to become a new state park, following the purchase of 650 acres by the Texas Parks and
articles.body: A family-owned ranch on Lake Palestine in East Texas is set to become a new state park, following the purchase of 650 acres by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Foundation. The October 2026 acquisition, reported by The Texas Tribune and supported by announcements from the Texas Parks and Wildlife Foundation and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, secures a substantial stretch of lakefront for future public recreation and conservation. The property in Henderson County has belonged to the Pollard family since 1940. Once associated with the family’s Texas Pecan Nursery business, the ranch has served as a place for growing pecans, hunting, fishing and gathering across generations. Its sale will turn a privately held family landscape into a public destination, although visitors will have to wait several years before the park is fully developed.A family legacy becomes public landFor the Pollard family, the transaction marks a significant change in the future of a property woven into its history. The ranch’s pecan orchard remains one of its defining features, alongside its wooded landscape and lake views. The sale was brokered by TexasLand, which represented the family. The property had been under contract for nearly a year while state officials conducted site visits, environmental assessments and planning evaluations to determine whether it could support a state park.The foundation completed the purchase for more than $10 million in October 2026. Rather than transferring the property immediately to the state, the nonprofit will hold the land until the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department can acquire it, a transaction currently anticipated for late 2027.Why the ranch stood outLocated approximately 18 miles west of Tyler and 20 miles east of Athens, the property includes roughly 2,000 feet of frontage on Lake Palestine. Its landscape combines pine forest, native grasses, a pecan orchard, a lake reaching depths of about 58 feet and approximately 10 ponds.The area also supports wildlife, including white-tailed deer, bobcats and waterfowl. Together, the natural habitat and extensive shoreline make the property suitable for a mix of conservation and outdoor recreation.For the state, acquiring the ranch would also create a public access point on a popular East Texas lake. Potential activities include boating, paddling, swimming and fishing, alongside hiking trails, campsites and day-use facilities. Scenic views from the lake’s bluffs could become another attraction.A funding strategy designed to protect the opportunityThe foundation’s interim ownership is intended to give the state more time to prepare for the purchase while allowing money in the Centennial Parks Conservation Fund to earn additional interest. Texas voters approved the $1 billion fund in 2023 to support the acquisition and development of parks. The delayed transfer would allow the state to use the fund when it is ready to take ownership and begin developing the site.The arrangement also illustrates how a conservation nonprofit can help secure land before public funding is ready to complete a transaction. By stepping in first, the foundation has helped prevent the opportunity from slipping away while the state completes its process.The park will open in stagesEven after the state takes ownership, the property will not immediately operate as a fully developed state park. Officials plan to begin with guided access before introducing day-use facilities and, eventually, overnight stays. The Texas Parks and Wildlife Department also intends to restore habitat and seek public input on how the property should be developed. Those steps will help determine the balance between recreational access and protecting the land’s ecological features.For the Pollard family, the sale offers a way for a place shaped by decades of private memories to serve a wider community. For Texas, it secures a large, largely undeveloped tract of lakefront that can be preserved while creating new opportunities for people to experience the outdoors.You use AI every day. By evening the Moon reaches Pisces, your sixth house of health and debts, joining Shani, your yogakaraka, which has been retrograde there for months. Exalted Jupiter aspects that house from your tenth, adding grace. A gentle Ekadashi fast gives the system a rest after a week of festival sweets. articles.title: Daughter of murdered woman 'refuses to be another victim'
articles.summary: Keeley McKee's mother Leanne was killed by her partner in 2003, weeks before the couple were due to marry.
articles.body:
A woman who was three years old when her mother was killed by her partner is speaking out about the damage caused by domestic abuse.

Keeley McKee only learned the full details of her mum Leanne's murder when she turned 18.

She is now channelling her pain into highlighting domestic abuse and the lasting impact it can have on those left behind, determined to turn her own experiences into something positive.

"I'm not being a victim of this story. I am going to do something about it," she said.

Warning: This story contains distressing details

Leanne McKee was killed by her partner in March 2003, weeks before the couple were due to marry. He then took his own life.

Keeley was staying with her grandmother that night and expected her mother to collect her the following day.

Her family protected her from the full circumstances of her mother's death as she grew up.

She said when she found out, it contributed to her spiralling out of control and abusing drugs and alcohol.

As a young child, Keeley remembers her mother telling her to hide in a bedroom and not come out until she was called.

"There was someone trying to get in, and I believe it was that partner that she was frightened of," Keeley told the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme.

At 18, she found a news report online about her mother's death and confronted what had happened.

"I had an idea but I think I was in denial. I didn't want to believe it and I didn't want to face it. I had googled it and saw a news article… I read it in the most brutal way you could probably read something like that.

"I think from that time then, I just ran away from grieving."

Keeley said she felt angry and confused, struggling to process the trauma.

She said her mental health deteriorated, she withdrew from friends and family, experienced suicidal thoughts and attempted to take her own life on multiple occasions.

She also struggled with drug and alcohol misuse and said the consequences of her mother's murder shaped how she viewed love and relationships.

"I was scared to fully love in case that was taken from me again," she added.

"For a while there, I didn't trust, but at the same time I've a lot of love to give.

"And I believe the right day God is going to put someone on my path, and I am going to build that strong family unit.

"And they're going to know nothing but love."

Keeley credits her faith with helping her confront the past after taking part in a Christian discipleship programme.

She said it allowed her to face the experiences she spent years avoiding.

"It gave me the fuel, it gave me the fight to say: 'I'm not being a victim of this anymore. My mum was a victim. I'm not being a victim of this story. I am going to do something about it'."

For Keeley, speaking up against domestic abuse is a way of living with her grief and seeking justice.

"My mum was robbed from me. The life that I had with my mum was taken from me by the evil acts of a man, who I won't name because I don't believe he deserves me to speak his name."

She added that she believes that violence has become normalised in society and said more needs to be done to tackle it.

She said she also wants greater recognition of the lasting impact domestic abuse has on the children and families left behind, saying they can be left struggling with trauma.

Keeley was brought up by her great-aunt and great-uncle, who took her into their home while they were grieving for Leanne themselves.

She said their support helped her through some of the most difficult periods of her life.

Now, she hopes her story will encourage people experiencing abuse to seek help and consider the impact on their children.

"Think about your future and your kids' future. What image is that giving them? You're bringing them up in an environment that they will see as normal and maybe they potentially treat their future partner the same way

"It's just going to go from generation to generation."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line .
